technical-data.invention-title: REAGENT AND METHOD FOR DETECTING AN ADULTERANT IN AN AQUEOUS SAMPLE
REACTIF ET PROCEDE UTILISES POUR DETECTER UN ADULTERANT DANS UN ECHANTILLON AQUEUX

abstract.p: This invention relates to a reagent and use of that reagent for detecting adulterants in aqueous samples, particularly in biological specimens such as urine samples using a diazo dye precursor such as N,N diethyl-1,4-phenylene diamine and a reagent such as creatinine to stabilize a colored intermediate formed by the reaction of the diamine with nitrite ions for a period sufficient to allow that color to be recorded and compared with a separate peak formed by a halogen-based oxidizing agent which may be present in solution.

Cette invention porte sur un réactif et sur l'utilisation de ce réactif détecter des adultérants dans des échantillons aqueux, en particulier dans des prélèvements biologiques tels que des échantillons d'urine, à l'aide d'un précurseur de colorant diazoïque tel que N,N diéthyle-1,4-phénylène diamine et d'un réactif tel que la créatinine pour stabiliser un intermédiaire coloré formé par la réaction de la diamine avec les ions de nitrite pendant une période suffisamment longue pour que l'on puisse enregistrer cette couleur et la comparer avec un pic séparé formé par un agent oxydant à base d'halogène qui peut se trouver en solution.

description.p: Reagent and Method for Detecting an Adulterant in an Aqueous Sample

Area of the Invention This invention relates to a reagent and use of that reagent for detecting adulterants in aqueous samples, particularly in biological specimens such as urine samples. Background of the Invention

Adulteration of uπne specimens has become an increasingly significant issue in urine drug testing. Products to mask the presence of drugs in the testing process are readily available and new products continue to emerge to stay in the forefront of technology. This invention provides a reagent that can be used in initial testing to screen for the presence of multiple adulterants. The ability of the reagent to detect multiple adulterants is significant because of the limited number of available reagent channels on the instruments used for analysis. This invention provides a reagent and method for detecting m a single, stable, test the presence or absence of three common adulterants: nitrites, pyπdmium chlorochromate and hypochloπtes like common bleach Summary of the Invention

In a first aspect this invention relates to a colorometπc method using a diazo dye precursor for distinguishing between the presence of a nitπte ion and a chloπne- contammg oxidizing agent in an aqueous solution, which method comprises adding to an aqueous solution a diazo dye precursor and an agent which stabilizes the colored intermediate formed by the reaction of the nitπte ion with the diazo dye precursor, reading and recording the absorbance of the solution at the peak corresponding to said intermediate formed by the nitπte/diazo dye precursor reaction and the peak corresponding to the color generated by the reaction of the chloπne-contammg oxidizing agent and the diazo dye precursor, and subtracting the absorbance of the peak corresponding to the chloπne adulterant from the absorbance of the peak corresponding to the intermediate formed by the mtπte/diazo dye precursor reaction, the readings being taken from a single container or optionally from two different containers.

In a second aspect, this invention relates to an improved colorometπc assay for detecting and distinguishing simultaneously in a single pot containing an aqueous solution the presence of a nitπte ion and a halogen-containing oxidizing agent using a diazo dye precursor wherein the improvement compπses using between about 0 1 and 10% weight/volume of a nucleophilic compound as the stabilizing agent for stabilizing the colored intermediate formed by the reaction of the diazo dye precursor and the
nitrite ion wherein the stabilized the intermediate is stabilized for at least about 1 minute or more.

In a third aspect this invention relates to a reagent for detecting simultaneously m an aqueous sample the presence of nitrites and chloπne-containmg oxidizing agents wherein the reagent compπses a diazo dye precursor and a nucleophile stabilizing agent Description of the Figures

Fig. 6 is a graphical representation of measured concentration vs spiked concentration data from an evaluation study involving solutions of sodium hypochlorite treated with DPD and creatmme Detailed Descπption of the Invention

This invention can be used in any situation requiπng the identification of the presence of nitπtes and halogen-containing oxidizing agents, particularly chloπne- containing oxidizing agents, in the same sample. It has particular applicability m identifying these two chemicals in aqueous samples where drug testing is involved, these two chemicals are added to samples to mask the presence of certain drugs or are added in hopes that they will interfere with the assays used to detect certain drugs. Drug testing is mandated or strongly support by many political and regulatory groups and private industry. Hiπng or continued employment may depend on a drug-free test. Urine-based testing is a widely practiced way of detecting the use of controlled substances or substances of abuse Not too surpπsmgly those who have found themselves placed in the predicament of having been exposed to certain drugs either purposefully or inadvertently and receiving a request for drug testing have identified and begun using chemicals which mask or interfere with the chemistries used to detect certain drugs. These are called adulterants. Most are chemicals which can be readily obtained by consumers, being that they have a number of uses and are readily available
through many consumer or retail channels. Adulterants now showing up with increasing frequency are nitπte salts and certain oxidizing agents, particularly certain chlorochromate salts and the alkali metal hypochloπtes, e.g., sodium hypochloπte or common bleach. This invention provides a way to distinguish between the nitπtes and oxidizing agents such as bleaches and chlorochromates m a one-step one-pot test. One aspect of the uniqueness of this assay is that it reads the absorbance of a stabilized intermediate formed by the nitrite ion and the diazo dye precursor rather than reading the absorbance of the diazo dye which forms as a result of reacting with the nitπte. In fact the diazo dye does not give a useful visible absorption spectrum. As a result of stabilizing the colored intermediate formed when the diazo dye precursor reacts with the nitπte ion and the oxidizing agent, two distinct absorbance peaks are obtained, one corresponding to the nitπte/diazo dye precursor intermediate and a second distinct peak corresponding to the oxidization product of the diazo dye precursor. And both can be recorded from the same sample at the same time. Thus the presence or absence of each distinct chemical can be determined and a concentration for each, if present, can be calculated for the same sample with just one pass.

The adulterants that this assay can usefully detect and distinguish between are nitπte salts and halogen-based oxidizing agents, particularly chloπne-containing bleaches such as the chlorochromate salts and the alkali metal salts of hypochlorus acid. The alkali metal salts of nitπte, particularly sodium nitπte, represent the most commonly encountered nitπte adulterants. Pyπdimum chlorochromate is the most commonly encountered chlorochromate adulterant. Common household bleach, sodium hypochlorite, is the most frequently encountered hypochlorite drug sample adulterant. Other halogen-based oxidizing agents can also be detected and distinguished using this invention.

A diazo dye precursor combined with a compound which is believed to stabilize the cherry-red colored intermediate formed by the reaction of the diazo dye precursor and the nitπte ion provides the basis for distinguishing between nitπte ions and halogen-based oxidizing agent.

In the context of this invention diazo dye precursors are thought to undergo a coupling reaction with nitπte ions to form a short-lived colored intermediate which then decays to a stable final product which has a different visible absorption spectra from that of the intermediate (Butler, R.M., Chem Rev, vol 75, p241 1975; Butler, R.M., JOC Perkins Trans, pi 357, 1973).

In the course of attempting to develop an assay to identify the presence of abnormal amounts of nitrites and/or oxidizing agents, it was observed that when the
diazo dye precursor N,N-dιethylphenylene diamine (DPD) was added to urme samples a cherry-red hue formed but faded m a matter of a few seconds followed by the development of a purple color, comonly refered to as a diazo tar. The latter color is useless for analytical purposes. It was thought that the fleeting cherry-red hue may have a visible absorption spectra which might be distinct from that of the visible absorption spectra observed in a urine sample containing a halogen-based oxidizing agent to which the dye precursor had been added. But because the cherry-red color was so fleeting it could not be used to generate reliable reproducible data. However it was noted that in a couple of uπne samples spiked with nitπte salts the cherry-red hue appeared to be a bit more persistent. On further investigation it was found that these samples shared a common phenomenon, each had a high creatinine level. Follow-up studies confirmed that adding creatinine stabilized the cherry-red color formed by adding the diazo dye to a mtπte-containmg uπne sample to a degree that allowed one to reliably and reproducible record the visible absorption spectra of that solution. This data showed that the stabilized DPD/nitπte color had an intense absorption peak at 411 nm and a weak absorption at 540 nm. This is important because samples with halogen-containing oxidizing agents to which DPD were added generated an intense absorption at around 540 nm.

Diazo dye precursors which can be used m this invention are the aromatic diammes such as the phenyl and naphthalene diammes which form diazo compounds under appropriate conditions and in the presence of certain chemicals. Generally speaking the precursors which are useful m this invention are the anilines, the ani nonaphthalenes and the likes of p-arsenihc acid which, when exposed to nitπte ions and halogen-based oxidizing agents, form intermediates exhibit a visible absorption spectra. While the para-substituted diammes usually exhibit the most intense color, ortho-substituted or meta-substituted diammes should work also. It is preferred that one of the nitrogens on the aromatic ring be mono or dialkylated, the other be substituted solely by hydrogen, so that only one of the nitrogens reacts with the nitπte ion and so that only diazo dyes are formed ultimately rather than polmeπzed lmmes. The following non-exhaustive list of compounds is believed to be illustrative of diazo dye precursors which can be used in this invention: N,N-dιethylphenylene diamme (DPD); 3-(4,5-dιmethylthιazolyl-2)-2,5-dιphenyl tetrazohum bromide, dimidium bromide; 2,4- dmιtro-l,8-naphthalenedιol; 2,4-dιmtro- 1 -naphthol; 2,2-dιphenyl-l-pιcrylhydrazyl; N- ethyl-N-(2-hydroxy-3-sulfopropyl)anιlιne; ethidium bromide; ethyl red; fast blue B, BB and RR and their salts; fast green dyes; fast red dyes; fast violet dyes; fast yellow dyes; cresol red; cresol blue; HABA; l-(2-hydroxyphenylazo)-2-hydroxyazobenzene; 3- methyl-N-ethyl-N-beta-hydroxyethylanilme; methylene blue, green or violet; methyl
green, orange, or red; mordant dyes; naphthol blue or green; n-(l- naphthyl)ethylenedιamme hydrochloπde; naphthly red; 1 -(p-nιtrophenylazo)-2- naphthol; pararosamlme; phenol red; / phenylazoamlme; o-phenylenediamme; l-(2- pyπdylazo)-2-naphthol; pyrocatechol violet; Sudan I, II, III or IN; 2-(2-thιazolyazo)-5- diemthylammophenol; l-(2-thιazolylazo)-2-naphthol; and 4-(2-thιazolylazo)resorcmol. DPD is most perferred.

The amount of diamine, or precursor, used will be some concentration which is sufficient to give a useful visible absorption spectra. Generally this will be some amount between about 0.7 and 0.9 mg per mL. Precursor is dissolved m a suitable solvent pπor to being added to the test sample. Various solvents can be used so long as the compound dissolves in it. For example when DPD is used it is convenient to first dissolve it m a short-chain organic acid such as formic acid or acetic acid before diluting it further with water.

The stabilizing agent used herein will be a compound that, when combined with a diazo dye, which m the presence of a nitπte ions m solution forms a colored intermediate, stabilizes that colored intermediate formed between the diazo dye and the nitπte ions react, to give a visible absorption spectra which persists for at least about 1 minute. This stabilizing agent is also called herein a nucleophilic compound. It is believed useful stabilizers will have a common characteπstic, that of having a pair of electrons to interact with and stabilize the transition state of the observed colored intermediate through which the diazo dye/nitπte reaction proceeds. This is a theoretical explanation of what has been observed; the invention is not to be limited by the theory of how the intermediate might be stabilized. Having discovered that creatinine stabilizes this colored intermediate it is believed other amines can also be used as stabilizing agents. Diethyl amine has been tested and gives equivocal results with DPD but may be efficacious when combined with other diazo dye precursors. Citric acid could used as well.

Time-wise, the color of the intermediate m a target sample should persist for several minutes. While it is recognized that some spectrophotometers can record rapid spectral events, m the context of routine chemical analyses time from sample preparation to spectral processing requires that the sample demonstrate the spectral event for a couple of minutes. And the event must be reliably reproducible so that data from at one time point can be compared against data at another time point. When the purplish color was first observed nitrite-spiked urme samples to which DPD had been added, the color was so fleeting that m was of no practical value to testing for adulterants. When it was discovered that nucleophiles could stabilize the transition state of the DPD/ tπte reaction, the target became that of creating a test in which the
color would persist for at least a mmute. That was achieved by identifying creatinine as a stabilizing agent and by manipulating the concentration of creatinine in the reaction pot. Time-wise, the color should persist for at least a minute. Preferably it will persist for at least 2 minutes. To achieve at least about 1 mmute of persistence in the color of the intermediate, about 0.1 and 10% by weight/volume of the nucleophile should be present in the test sample.

A preferred embodiment of this invention is one where the dye is N,N- dimethylphenylene diamine (DPD) and creatinine as the stabilizing nucleophile. DPD is available commercially. It is can be purchased from Sigma-Aldπch or ICN Biochemicals.

When a nitπte salt is present the nitrite ion reacts with DPD to produce an intermediate which has an intense absorption peak at 411 nm and a weak absoption peak at 540 nm. If a chlorochromate or hypochloπte ions are present the reaction with DPD produces an intense absorption peak at 540 nm. These two distinct absorption maxima provide a means for distinguishing between nitrites and oxidizing agents. As a practical matter, the cherry-red color of the nitπte/DPD intermediate is measured at 410 nm. In fact the measurement of the cherry-red color can be vaπed around the 411 nm maximum up to ±5 nm without loss of sensitivity or accuracy. Similarly the 540 nm maximum peak can be read at ±5 nm without loss of sensitivity or accuracy as well. Having identified the existence of a second measurable maximum at 411 nm, the precise choice wavelength in that area of the visible spectrum and that surrounding the 540 nm maximum of the oxidization product is within the skill of the practitioner. The following examples are provide to illustrate the invention but are not intended to limit it in any fashion or to any degree.

Example 1 DPD/Creatimne Reagent A reagent for detecting the presence of nitπtes, chlorochromates or hypochloπtes is prepared as follows: Creatinine (2 gm) is dissolved m 200 mL deiomzed water and a quantity of deionized water sufficient to make a volume of 500 mL. Then 0.4 gm of N,N diethyl- 1,4-phenylene diamine is dissolved in 30 mL of glacial acetic acid. To this solution is then added enough of the creatinine solution prepared above to give a volume of 500 mL. This solution is then ready for use in the colorometπc assay for detecting nitπte and chlorine-containing adulterants.
Example 2 Figures 1 and 2 set out the visible spectra for the DPD reagent prepared m Example 1 when sodium nitπte, sodium hypochlorite and pyπdinium chlorochromate are added. The visible spectra of the dye that forms with sodium hypochloπte is identical to the visible spectra of the dye that forms from the reaction with pyπdinium chlorochromate. It can easily be seen that the sodium nitrite produces a dye with intense absorption at about 41 1 nm and a weak absorption at around 540 nm. Sodium hypochlorite generates an intense absorption only at 540 nm as does pyπdinium chlorochromate. A useful analytical method results which gives positive absorbance for sodium nitrite and negative absorbance for sodium hypochloπte and pyπdinium chlorochromate. The method is useful for concentrations of sodium nitπte above two thousand PPM. High concentrations of sodium hypochloπte (20% solutions) increases the lifetime of the cherry-red dye. Example 2 Validation Studies Validation studies were performed to evaluate the following parameters for nitπte, pyndinium chlorochromate and sodium hypochlorite:
Linearity - the linear range at multiple concentration ranges above and below the cutoff were evaluated.

Precision - Intra-run precision was evaluated at the concentration ranges used for linearity evaluation. Inter-run precision was evaluated on quality control samples spiked at +25 % and -25 % of cutoff.
Correlation- Nitrite: Specimens were tested for nitrite using a current nitrite reagent and DPD and creatinine as prepared in Example 1
Pyndinium Chlorochromate: Specimens tested for pyndinium chlorochromate and found to be positive were also evaluated by gas chromatography/mass specfrometry to confirm the presence of the adulterant.

Sodium hypochlorite (bleach): Specimen were tested for bleach and found to be positive were also evaluated using an AquaCheck dipstick to confirm the presence of chloπne. Carryover - High concentrations of nitrite, pyndinium chlorochromate and bleach were evaluated along with negative controls to determine the level at which carryover occurs in the testing process.

Olympus AU 5061 and AU800 chemistry analyzers were used for recording absorbance spectra. In each of these assays the target adulterant was spiked into deionized water for nitrite and urine for pyndinium chlorochromate and bleach and then DPD/creatimne reagent prepared as per Example 1 was added as descπbed below.
